sections.title: SLOs, observability, security, disaster recovery and failure reviews

topics.title: Availability in nines and downtime budgets

kcs.statement: Availability is the fraction of time (or of requests) a system serves successfully: uptime / (uptime + downtime).
99.9% availability allows about 8.77 hours of downtime per year (about 43.8 minutes per month); each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by 10×.

serves.reason: The o5 product ends in an availability figure expressed in nines.

problem_ideas: Convert 99.95% into minutes of allowed downtime per month
A service was down 4 hours last year: how many nines did it achieve?
How much downtime per week does four nines allow?
A deploy causes a 2-minute outage each release; how many releases per month fit in a 99.99% budget?
Request-based: 1.2 billion requests, 300,000 failed. What is the availability?

lens.reason: Interviewers expect you to translate 'highly available' into a nines figure and a downtime budget.

topics.title: Availability in series and in parallel

kcs.statement: Components in series (all must work) have availability equal to the probability that all of them are up at once; only when their failures are independent is this the product of their availabilities, so two independent 99.9% components give about 99.8%.
Redundant components in parallel (any one suffices) have availability 1 − (1 − A)^n when their failures are independent: two independent 99.9% replicas give 99.9999%.

Both the series product and the parallel formula assume independent failures; a shared dependency such as one power feed, one region or one config push correlates failures, so replicas fail together and the parallel figure overstates availability, and the shared dependency must be counted as its own component in series.

serves.reason: Computing the availability figure for a design requires combining tiers in series and in parallel.

requires.reason: The results are stated and compared in nines.

topics.title: Reliability, high availability and fault tolerance

kcs.statement: Availability measures whether the system is up when asked; reliability measures whether it performs correctly over time, so a system can be up yet unreliable when it returns wrong results.

High availability minimises downtime by recovering quickly and accepts a brief blip during failover; fault tolerance keeps operating with no interruption through a failure, at higher cost through full redundancy.

topics.title: Finding and removing single points of failure

kcs.statement: A single point of failure is any component whose failure alone takes the whole system down; find them by tracing the request path and asking what happens if each component dies.

Remove a single point of failure by adding redundancy, such as a second load balancer sharing a floating IP, database replicas or several app servers, including often-forgotten ones such as DNS, a single region or one config service.

serves.reason: o5 asks for a list of single points of failure in a design.

requires.reason: Redundancy is justified by the parallel availability formula.

problem_ideas: List every SPOF in: one LB → 3 app servers → one Postgres primary

A single Redis instance holds sessions: what breaks when it restarts?

topics.title: Health checks and heartbeats

kcs.statement: A load balancer sends periodic health checks to each backend, removes a backend from the pool after N consecutive failures and adds it back after it passes again.
With heartbeats, a node is declared dead after its heartbeats are missing for a timeout; a short timeout detects failures faster but causes false positives during slow networks or GC pauses.

problem_ideas: Checks every 5 s with 3 failures to evict: worst-case seconds of traffic sent to a dead server

topics.title: Failover: active-passive and active-active

kcs.statement: In active-passive failover a standby takes over the active node's role (often its IP) when heartbeats stop; downtime is detection time plus promotion time, and a hot standby recovers faster than a cold one.
In active-active, all nodes serve traffic and a failed node's load is redistributed, so each node must keep enough headroom to absorb its share.
Failing over to an asynchronously replicated database replica can lose the writes that had not yet replicated when the primary died.

serves.reason: Failover is the named fix for most single points of failure in o5.

requires.reason: Failover is triggered by health checks or missed heartbeats.
Failover is presented as the fix for a single point of failure.

problem_ideas: Two active-active servers each at 70% CPU: what happens when one fails?

topics.title: Timeouts and cascading failures

kcs.statement: Every remote call needs a timeout; without one, a hung dependency holds threads or connections until the caller's pool is exhausted and the failure cascades upstream.
Set a call's timeout from the dependency's tail latency (a little above its p99) and below the caller's own deadline, so the caller still has time to respond or fall back.

problem_ideas: 200 threads, a dependency hangs, 50 req/s arrive: how many seconds until the pool is exhausted?
A dependency's p99 is 120 ms; the API deadline is 500 ms with 3 downstream calls in sequence. Set timeouts.

Should a timeout on a write be retried? What do you need to know?

lens.reason: Timeouts underpin retries and circuit breakers, which interviewers ask about directly.

topics.title: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter

kcs.statement: Exponential backoff doubles the wait between retries (for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms) up to a cap, giving a struggling dependency time to recover.
Jitter randomises each backoff delay (for example uniformly between 0 and the computed delay) so clients that failed together do not retry in synchronised waves.
Retry only transient errors (timeouts, 503, 429) and only idempotent operations or calls carrying an idempotency key, with a cap on attempts so retries do not become a retry storm.

serves.reason: Retries with backoff are one of the fixes o5 explicitly names.

requires.reason: A retry is triggered by a timeout and must fit inside the caller's deadline.
Whether a call is safe to retry depends on idempotency.

problem_ideas: Write backoff_delays(base_ms, factor, cap_ms, attempts) returning the delay schedule

topics.title: Circuit breakers: failing fast

kcs.statement: A circuit breaker stays closed (calls pass) until failures exceed a threshold, then opens (calls fail immediately without reaching the dependency), then after a cool-down goes half-open, where a few trial calls decide whether to close or reopen.
Failing fast while the breaker is open stops the caller from wasting threads on a dead dependency and gives the dependency room to recover, preventing a cascading failure.
While the breaker is open, the caller returns a fallback such as cached data, a default or a degraded response instead of an error, where the product allows it.

serves.reason: The circuit breaker is one of the fixes o5 explicitly names.

requires.reason: Timeouts are the failures the breaker counts and the cascade it prevents.

kcs.statement: A bulkhead gives each dependency or workload its own isolated pool of threads, connections or instances, so exhaustion in one cannot starve the others.

topics.title: Microservices vs monoliths

kcs.statement: Microservices split an application into independently deployable services, each owning its own data and communicating over the network through APIs or messages.
Microservices buy independent scaling and deployment at the cost of network latency, partial failures, distributed transactions and harder debugging, so a monolith is often the right starting point.
Services that share one database or must be deployed together form a distributed monolith: they carry the costs of distribution without the independence.

problem_ideas: Split a ride-hailing app into services and name each one's data

topics.title: Distributed transactions and two-phase commit

kcs.statement: In two-phase commit a coordinator first asks every participant to prepare (each votes yes only after durably recording its changes and holding locks), then sends commit if all voted yes and abort otherwise.
Two-phase commit is blocking: if the coordinator fails after participants voted yes, they keep holding locks and cannot decide on their own until it recovers.
Two-phase commit gives atomicity across stores at the cost of latency and availability, so it suits a few tightly coupled databases, not long-running business flows across services.

requires.reason: 2PC extends the atomicity of a local transaction across nodes.

problem_ideas: Trace 2PC message by message for a transfer between two bank shards

topics.title: Sagas and compensating transactions

kcs.statement: A saga splits a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensating transaction that semantically undoes it if a later step fails.
In an orchestrated saga a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next; in a choreographed saga each service reacts to events from the previous step, with no central controller.
Unlike two-phase commit, a saga holds no locks across steps, so other requests can see intermediate states, and its steps and compensations must be idempotent because they may be retried.

requires.reason: Sagas are defined and justified in contrast to two-phase commit.

problem_ideas: Write the steps and compensations for order → reserve stock → charge card → ship

topics.title: Leader election, split brain and fencing

kcs.statement: Leader election picks exactly one node to perform a role, such as accepting writes or running a scheduler, and picks a new one when heartbeats show the leader is gone.
Split brain happens when a network partition lets two nodes both believe they are leader; requiring votes from a majority prevents it because only one side of a partition can hold a majority.
A leader holds a time-limited lease, and a fencing token (a number that increases with each new leader) lets storage reject writes from a stale former leader whose lease has expired.

requires.reason: Leader failure is detected through missed heartbeats.

problem_ideas: A cron scheduler runs on 3 nodes: how do you make each job run once?

topics.title: Consensus in one idea: Raft and coordination services

kcs.statement: Consensus algorithms such as Raft and Paxos let a cluster agree on a value or log order; a cluster of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures, so 5 nodes survive 2.
Designs rarely implement consensus directly; they use a coordination service built on it, such as ZooKeeper or etcd, for leader election, locks and configuration.

requires.reason: Consensus is presented as the safe mechanism behind leader election.
Majority-based fault tolerance builds on quorum sizes.

topics.title: SLAs, SLOs, SLIs and error budgets

kcs.statement: An SLI is a measured indicator (for example the share of requests served under 300 ms), an SLO is the internal target for it (99.9%), and an SLA is the external contract with penalties, usually set looser than the SLO.
The error budget is 1 − SLO: at a 99.9% monthly SLO, about 43 minutes of downtime or 0.1% of requests may fail before releases should slow down.
SLIs should be chosen from the user's view of the stated non-functional requirements, such as availability, latency or freshness, so each SLO maps to one requirement.

requires.reason: SLO targets and error budgets are expressed in nines and downtime.

problem_ideas: 10 million requests this month, SLO 99.95%: how many failures are allowed?

topics.title: Monitoring: metrics, logs, traces and alerts

kcs.statement: Observability rests on three signals: metrics (cheap numeric time series for dashboards and alerts), logs (detailed records of individual events) and traces (one request's path across services).
The four golden signals to monitor for any service are latency, traffic, errors and saturation, and alerts should fire on user-facing symptoms such as SLO burn rather than on every internal cause.

topics.title: Security overview: authn, authz, encryption, abuse

kcs.statement: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization decides whether that identity may perform this action on this specific resource, so it must be checked by the service that owns the resource, not only at the edge.

An API gateway validates the caller's signed access token once at ingress (signature, expiry and audience), rejects invalid requests with 401, and forwards the verified identity to internal services, which still enforce authorization and return 403 when access is denied.

Encrypt data in transit with TLS from client to edge and TLS or mTLS between internal services, and limit abuse with per-user or per-key rate limiting, input validation and least-privilege credentials for each service.

requires.reason: Token validation at ingress is placed on the API gateway.
Transport encryption builds on TLS, TLS termination and mTLS.

topics.title: Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO and DR strategies

kcs.statement: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (how old the last good copy may be); RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disaster.

Disaster recovery strategies trade cost for recovery speed: backup and restore (cheapest, RTO of hours), cold site, warm standby, and hot site or multi-region active-active (most expensive, RTO of seconds to minutes).
Nightly backups give an RPO of up to 24 hours, continuous asynchronous replication to another region shrinks RPO to the replication lag, and synchronous replication brings it near zero.

requires.reason: DR strategies are failover at the scale of a site or region.
RPO is derived from the replication mode.

topics.title: Failure-mode review of a design under time

kcs.statement: A failure-mode review walks each component on the request path and names what happens when it dies, slows down or is cut off by a partition.

Each failure maps to a standard fix: a single point of failure to redundancy and failover, a slow dependency to a timeout plus a circuit breaker, a transient error to retry with backoff and jitter, and a duplicate request to an idempotency key.

End-to-end availability is estimated by collapsing each redundant tier with the parallel formula and multiplying the tiers in series, both valid only for independent failures, so shared dependencies such as one region or one config service are added as their own series components before converting the result to nines and yearly downtime.
In an interview, reliability belongs in the bottlenecks phase: name the top two or three failure modes of your design and their fixes rather than listing every pattern.

serves.reason: This topic produces o5's observable product: SPOF list, fixes and an availability figure.
The bottlenecks and failure part of a full mock interview is practised here.

requires.reason: The review computes end-to-end availability.
Failover is the fix for most identified SPOFs.
